title: Preventing Falls at Home
hook: Falls are the leading cause of injury for older adults, but most are preventable with a few targeted fixes.
key_points: Falls are the top cause of injury and injury death among older adults.
Remove trip hazards: loose rugs, clutter, and cords in walkways.
Add grab bars in the bathroom, railings on stairs, and brighter lighting.
Strength and balance exercises lower fall risk.
Review medicines and check vision; both can affect balance and steadiness.
content_html: Falls are the leading cause of injury and injury-related death among older adults, but they are not an inevitable part of aging. The CDC's STEADI program is built around the idea that most falls can be prevented by addressing a handful of known risk factors.
extra_html:
Start with the home itself. Remove trip hazards like loose rugs, clutter, and cords across walkways. Add grab bars by the toilet and in the shower, install sturdy handrails on both sides of stairs, and improve lighting, especially on stairs and the path to the bathroom at night.

Beyond the home, the CDC highlights the body and its inputs. Strength and balance exercises directly reduce fall risk, so staying active matters. Ask a clinician or pharmacist to review medicines, since some cause dizziness or drowsiness, and keep vision checked and glasses up to date. Together, these steps make a meaningful dent in fall risk.

source.name: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (STEADI)

related.title: Staying Strong as You Age
related.hook: The decline we associate with old age is partly the result of doing less. Staying active — in four distinct ways — keeps you independent far longer.

related.title: Protecting Your Bones
related.hook: Bone looks permanent, but it's living tissue that thins with age. Osteoporosis weakens it silently until a minor fall causes a major break.

related.title: Why Strength Training Matters
related.hook: Cardio gets the glory, but lifting, resistance bands, and bodyweight moves protect something running can't: the muscle and bone you'll rely on for decades.

related.title: Taking Medicines Safely
related.hook: Medicines help only when used right. Most medication mishaps are preventable with a few habits — reading the label, knowing your list, and asking questions.

flashcards.prompt: Name three ways to reduce fall risk for an older adult at home.
flashcards.back_html: Remove trip hazards (loose rugs, clutter, cords), add grab bars and stair railings with better lighting, do strength and balance exercises, and review medicines and vision with a clinician.

flashcards.prompt: Which of these is part of preventing falls in older adults?

choices.text: Reviewing medicines that can affect balance
Avoiding all physical activity to prevent injury
Keeping rooms dim to reduce glare

flashcards.explanation_html: Some medicines cause dizziness or drowsiness, so a review can cut fall risk. Staying active builds the strength and balance that prevent falls, and good lighting helps, so avoiding activity and keeping rooms dim would backfire.
